organism: Influenza is a single-stranded RNA virus of the orthomyxovirus family. Three types affect humans: A (subtyped by hemagglutinin and neuraminidase surface antigens, with 8 H and 6 N subtypes detected in humans), B (two lineages, Yamagata and Victoria), and C (rarely causes reported illness and has not been linked to epidemics). Surface antigens change continually through antigenic drift (small, gradual mutations that let the virus evade existing immunity - the main reason people get influenza repeatedly and why vaccine composition is reviewed every year) and, more rarely, antigenic shift (an abrupt, major change in a surface antigen, usually via genetic recombination between influenza A viruses, that can spark a pandemic).
clinicalFeaturesSummary: Incubation period is usually 2 days (range 1-4). About 8% of the US population gets symptomatically ill each season (range 3%-11%). Onset is sudden: respiratory symptoms (cough, sore throat, runny or stuffy nose) alongside systemic symptoms (fever, chills, headache, malaise, myalgia), with vomiting and diarrhea more common in children. Recovery is usually rapid - fever resolves in 3-4 days, other symptoms in about a week - though some lingering weakness can persist for weeks. Aspirin and other salicylates should be avoided in children and adolescents because of the Reye syndrome risk. Complications include secondary bacterial pneumonia, exacerbation of underlying respiratory disease, otitis media, and less commonly encephalitis, myocarditis, Guillain-Barre syndrome, and Reye syndrome; those 65 and older, people with chronic medical conditions, pregnant people, and children under 5 (especially under 2) are at highest risk for serious complications, and most influenza deaths occur in people 65 and older.
epidemiologySummary: Humans are the only known reservoir for influenza C; influenza B mostly infects humans (rarely documented in seals); influenza A infects humans and various animals (wild birds, poultry, pigs, horses, mink, ferrets), with no chronic carrier state. Transmission is primarily via large respiratory droplets from coughing or sneezing landing on mucosal surfaces within about 6 feet, with aerosol transmission of smaller droplets and indirect contact with contaminated surfaces also playing a role. In the Northern Hemisphere, season typically runs October through April/May and most often peaks in January or later; the Southern Hemisphere's season runs April-September, and tropical regions see influenza year-round. Adults can transmit from the day before symptoms start through about 5-7 days after; children can remain contagious for 10 or more days.
secularTrendsSummary: CDC estimates 9.3 to 45 million people experience symptomatic illness in the US annually. Since 2010, estimated annual influenza-associated deaths have ranged from 12,447 (2011-2012) to 61,099 (2017-2018), averaging 37,463, with people 65+ accounting for about 80% of deaths; the 2019-2020 season had a record 189 reported pediatric deaths. Influenza causes more hospitalizations in young children than any other vaccine-preventable disease (an estimated 7,000-26,000 annually in children under 5 since 2010). Vaccination coverage varies widely by age group and season - during 2019-2020, coverage ranged from about 42% in adults 18-64 to about 70% in adults 65+ and about 75% in young children. CDC estimates vaccination averted about 4.9 million symptomatic illnesses, 70,000 hospitalizations, and 6,400 deaths across the 2010-2011 through 2017-2018 seasons. Pandemics (from antigenic shift) are rare - five have occurred since the late 19th century (1889-1891, 1918-1920, 1957-1958, 1968-1969, 2009-2010); the 1918-1919 'Spanish flu' pandemic caused an estimated 21 million deaths worldwide, and the 2009 H1N1 pandemic caused illness in more than 60 million Americans, notably shifting 90% of hospitalizations and deaths to people under 65.
vaccineDescription: Three vaccine types are licensed in the US: inactivated influenza vaccine (IIV, available since the 1940s, most commonly egg-grown though cell-culture-based products also exist, given intramuscularly), recombinant influenza vaccine (RIV, first licensed 2013, produced without egg-grown virus and containing no egg protein, given intramuscularly), and live attenuated influenza vaccine (LAIV, first licensed 2003, egg-grown, cold-adapted, given intranasally). Quadrivalent formulations (three type A/B strains plus an extra B lineage) have been standard since the 2013-2014 season. Because the virus changes constantly, vaccine composition, specific product contraindications, and ACIP recommendations are reviewed and reissued every single season - this chapter's schedule, safety, and contraindication summaries describe the general pattern, not a fixed, permanent formulation.
vaccinationScheduleSummary: Annual vaccination is recommended for everyone 6 months and older without contraindications. People 9 and older need 1 dose each season. Children 6 months through 8 years need 2 doses at least 4 weeks apart if they lack documentation of 2 or more prior influenza vaccine doses before July 1 of that season; otherwise, 1 dose suffices. CDC recommends vaccination by the end of October, but vaccine should keep being offered throughout the season since timing of onset and peak varies year to year - vaccinating very early (July/August) is associated with reduced protection later in the season, especially in older adults. LAIV should not be given on the same day as another live vaccine unless truly simultaneous; otherwise, a 4-week gap is needed between them.
vaccineEfficacySummary: Immunity is functionally short-lived - under a year - because of both antibody waning and antigenic drift in circulating strains, which is why vaccination is needed every season rather than being a one-time or periodic booster. Overall effectiveness against illness is typically 40%-60% when vaccine strains closely match circulating strains, though it has ranged from as low as 19% to as high as 60% in recent seasons depending on strain match, and tends to be lower in adults 65 and older. Even when it doesn't fully prevent illness, vaccination is associated with fewer medical visits, ICU/hospital admissions, and (in children) fewer deaths, as well as reduced severity of breakthrough illness.
contraindicationsSummary: For IIV and RIV: a severe allergic reaction to a vaccine component or a prior dose is a contraindication; moderate or severe acute illness is a precaution, as is a history of Guillain-Barre syndrome within 6 weeks of a prior influenza vaccine dose (a precaution across all licensed influenza vaccines). LAIV carries additional product-specific contraindications and precautions that, like the vaccine formulation itself, are reissued each season - always check that season's current ACIP recommendations rather than relying on a prior year's list. LAIV is specifically contraindicated during pregnancy; people at high risk for influenza complications (e.g. immunosuppressed people, or those with chronic pulmonary or cardiac disease) should receive IIV or RIV rather than LAIV, since LAIV safety data in those groups is limited.
vaccineSafetySummary: IIV: local reactions (soreness, redness, tenderness, swelling) are common, with pain reported by up to 65% of recipients in the first week; systemic symptoms (fever, chills, malaise, myalgia) are less common and, per recent data, no more frequent than with placebo. IIV has been associated with a modestly increased febrile-seizure risk in young children, especially when co-administered with PCV13 and DTaP on the same day - ACIP reviewed this and did not change same-day administration recommendations, since most febrile seizures are brief with a good prognosis. Long-term safety monitoring has not established a clear link to Guillain-Barre syndrome; if any excess risk exists, it's estimated at no more than 1-2 cases per million doses, smaller than the GBS risk associated with influenza illness itself. RIV: in trials, the most common reactions were injection-site tenderness (48%) and pain (37%), plus headache, fatigue, and muscle pain; postlicensure VAERS review found no new safety signal. LAIV: most common reactions were runny nose/congestion (all ages), fever (children 2-6), and sore throat (adults); safety data in high-risk groups (immunosuppressed, chronic pulmonary/cardiac disease) remain limited.
vaccineStorageSummary: IIV, RIV, and LAIV must all be stored at refrigerator temperature, 2C to 8C (36F to 46F); LAIV sprayers must stay in their carton until use to protect them from light. See CDC's Vaccine Storage and Handling Toolkit for complete guidance.
surveillanceSummary: Influenza-associated deaths in people under 18 and human infection with a novel influenza A virus are nationally notifiable through NNDSS; other influenza infections are not nationally notifiable but may be reportable in individual states. US influenza surveillance spans five categories - viral, outpatient illness, mortality, hospitalization, and geographic spread - aimed at tracking circulating strains for vaccine formulation, estimating disease burden, detecting outbreaks, and guiding rapid control measures. See CDC's Manual for the Surveillance of Vaccine-Preventable Diseases for general reporting guidance.

supplementalTopics.title: Vaccination During Pregnancy
supplementalTopics.summary: Pregnant people face increased risk of severe influenza illness and complications due to pregnancy-related changes in immune, heart, and lung function, and influenza infection has been linked in some studies to preterm delivery and fetal demise. ACIP and ACOG recommend that anyone who is pregnant, might be pregnant, or is up to 2 weeks postpartum during influenza season receive any licensed, age-appropriate IIV or RIV product - vaccination can happen at any point in pregnancy. LAIV is contraindicated during pregnancy.

supplementalTopics.title: Annual Reformulation - A Living Recommendation
supplementalTopics.summary: Unlike most other vaccines in this library, influenza vaccine composition, and even some contraindication and precaution details (particularly for LAIV), are reviewed and reissued by ACIP every single season based on which strains are circulating and how well the prior season's vaccine performed. Any consumer of this content should treat the schedule/safety/contraindication summaries here as describing the general, recurring pattern - not a fixed formulation - and check CDC's current-season ACIP recommendations (https://www.cdc.gov/vaccines/hcp/acip-recs/vacc-specific/flu.html) for the specifics of any given year.

keyPoints: The name 'influenza' comes from 15th-century Italy, attributing epidemics to the 'influence of the stars'
Antigenic drift (gradual mutation) causes annual epidemics and requires yearly vaccine reformulation; antigenic shift (abrupt major change) causes rare pandemics - 5 since the late 1800s
Influenza causes more hospitalizations in young children than any other vaccine-preventable disease
Vaccine effectiveness against illness is typically 40%-60%, but varies substantially by season depending on how well vaccine strains match circulating strains
Protection lasts under a year, so annual revaccination is needed regardless of prior-season vaccination
LAIV is contraindicated in pregnancy and not preferred for people at high risk of complications - IIV or RIV should be used instead
Only pediatric influenza deaths and novel influenza A infections are nationally notifiable; most influenza cases are not
